en: The Sūtra on the Adornment of Wisdom that Transcends the Realms of All Buddhas, translated by the Tripitaka Master Saṃghavarman of Funan during the Liang Dynasty, together with others.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was dwelling atop Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the city of Rājagṛha.

Above the palace of the realm, together with a great assembly of twenty-five thousand bhikṣus—all of whom were arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions; whose minds were well-liberated and whose wisdom was well-liberated; who had tamed their faculties like great elephants (mahānāga); who had done what was to be done and accomplished what was to be accomplished; who had laid down the heavy burden and attained their own goal; whose fetters were exhausted and who had attained mastery over their minds—namely, Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the others, along with the eight great śrāvakas.
Furthermore, there were seventy-two billion nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, whose names were:

Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Śubhakārin Bodhisattva, Buddhaśrī Bodhisattva, Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva, Nityotthita Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, and others. They were capable of turning the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma and skillfully inquiring into the *Anupamaratnakūṭa-sūtra* and other scriptures. Dwelling on the stage of Dharmameghā, their wisdom was like Mount Sumeru; they constantly practiced the profound illumination of the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, and lack of intrinsic nature. With perfected merit and complete dignified deportment, they had been dispatched by Tathāgatas from countless nayutas of worlds, possessing great supernormal powers and abiding in the markless nature of reality.
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:

"These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have come here from worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; I shall preach the Dharma for them so that they may attain great power, and I shall manifest signs of supernatural power and emit great radiance, because these bodhisattvas are about to question me."

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a great radiance, universally illuminating immeasurable, inconceivable worlds as numerous as the dust motes in a trichiliocosm throughout the ten directions.

At that moment, from each of the ten directions across ten Buddha-worlds, there came bodhisattvas as numerous as the dust motes in unspeakably many thousands of myriads of kotis of nayutas. Each had departed from their own realm, riding upon inconceivable and immeasurable supernormal powers, and had assembled here. They further made offerings to the Tathāgata with inconceivable articles of worship and sat before the Buddha upon lotus thrones fashioned according to their own inclinations, gazing up at the World-Honored One without ever averting their eyes.

At that time, above the palace of the Dharma-realm, there arose a great lion-throne within a jewel-lotus treasury, immeasurable billions of yojanas in length and breadth, composed of countless radiant mani-jewels.

It was interlaced with electric lamp-maṇi jewels, had poles made of maṇi jewels of inconceivable power, and was accompanied by maṇi jewels beyond analogy; it was adorned with maṇi jewels surpassing all analogies, featured a canopy of sovereign king maṇi jewels, and was inlaid with various miscellaneous maṇi gems. Various colored banners were suspended from it, and it was surrounded by great maṇi jewels that emitted ten kinds of immeasurable billions of nayutas of light rays, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.

At that time, an inexpressible number of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of atoms—equal in number to the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the four heavenly kings—came from ten buddha-worlds in the ten directions and assembled here.

Furthermore, there were various devas riding in palaces with jeweled spires; accompanied by countless, inconceivable numbers of celestial maidens, they performed hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of musical performances and also gathered here.

Furthermore, there were various devas who arrived at this assembly riding in palaces of precious lotuses; palaces of naga-jewel sandalwood and divine pearls; palaces of pearl; palaces of precious raiment; palaces of *maṇi* jewels of golden light; palaces of Jambūnada gold; palaces of *maṇi* jewels of immeasurable radiance; palaces of sovereign-kings *maṇi* jewels; palaces of wish-fulfilling *maṇi* jewels; palaces of *maṇi* jewels that surpass Śakra; and palaces of great *maṇi* jewels with crowns of mind, adorned with pure jewels from the ocean’s depths and emitting universal light. Accompanied by countless, inconceivable billions of *nayutas* of celestial maidens, they came together to this gathering while performing various musical performances.

All of them made offerings to the Buddha with countless, inconceivable articles; having made these offerings, they each sat down as they pleased, gazing up at the World-Honored One without ever averting their eyes for a moment.

At that time, this great trichiliocosm became entirely the golden color of Jambudvīpa; it was adorned with various *maṇi* jewel trees—trees of celestial flowers, trees of precious robes, and trees of dragon-jewel sandalwood—and was draped with networks of *maṇi* jewels such as the sun, moon, and lightning-lamps, which completely covered the world. Various banners were suspended everywhere, and countless thousands of millions of billions of *nayuta*s of celestial maidens held various necklaces and various precious flowers.
At that time, from the great precious lotus lion throne, these verses issued forth:
"You all are now seated at ease; I shall speak the truth.
This lion throne of the King of Men was fashioned from the merits of the Tathāgata."
Today my wish is fulfilled as I make offerings to the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings.
May the World-Honored One now sit upon a lotus throne of the seven treasures;
may he emit great rays of light that illuminate me and all beings.
He preaches the unsurpassed, sublime Dharma, benefiting all devas and humans;
those sentient beings who hear this Dharma shall sit upon the lion throne.
Such great radiance as this issues forth from the body of the Tathāgata.
Illuminating immeasurable worlds, causing all to rejoice;
the Teacher, God among Gods, should now accept me.
In the past, at this very place, I encountered eight hundred million Buddhas.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will now, out of compassion, graciously accept us.

At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat of radiance and sat upon the lion throne within the treasury of precious lotuses. Sitting cross-legged, he observed that the assembly of bodhisattvas had all gathered; for the sake of inspiring these bodhisattvas, he was about to expound the Dharma of emptiness.
At that time, the bodhisattvas had this thought:
"This youth Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva shall question the Tathāgata regarding non-arising and non-ceasing; we have not heard this Dharma for a very long time."
At that time, Mañjuśrī, already knowing the Tathāgata’s intention to teach the characteristics of dharmas as well as the thoughts in the minds of all the bodhisattvas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"What are the characteristics of the dharmas that are neither born nor extinguished? Mañjuśrī spoke this geya:
"How can that which is neither born nor extinguished be known?"
O Great Muni, please provide an analogy.
This great assembly has all gathered here; they delight in hearing this meaning and pray that the Buddha will explain it.
"Now these bodhisattvas, sent by all the Buddhas, also all delight in hearing the subtle and wondrous characteristics of the Dharma.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
"Excellent, excellent!"
The question you have now asked is able to bring great benefit to all the world and enables all bodhisattvas to perform the work of a Buddha.
Mañjuśrī! You should listen attentively and not give rise to alarm or doubt.
Mañjuśrī! That which is neither born nor extinguished is the Tathāgata. Mañjuśrī!
For example, suppose the great earth were composed of lapis lazuli, such that the reflections of Śakra’s Vaijayanta Palace, its furnishings, and other objects appeared within it.
People of Jambudvīpa, seeing the reflections of those various palaces upon the lapis lazuli ground, would join their palms in worship, burn incense, and scatter flowers, saying:
"May I be born in such palaces; may I sport therein like Śakra and the others."

Those sentient beings do not know that this place is the reflection of a palace; they instead practice giving, maintain the precepts, and cultivate various meritorious virtues in order to obtain the retribution of such a palace.
Mañjuśrī! These palaces are in truth without arising or ceasing; they appear as reflections therein because the ground is pure.
Those palace-reflections both exist and do not exist, neither arising nor ceasing.
“Mañjuśrī! The perception of sentient beings regarding the Buddha is likewise.

Because their minds are pure, they see the body of the Buddha; the Buddha-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), neither arising nor originating, neither ceasing nor perishing; it is neither form (*rūpa*) nor non-form, neither visible nor invisible, neither worldly nor non-worldly, neither mind (*citta*) nor non-mind. Sentient beings, because their minds are pure, see the body of the Tathāgata and offer various kinds of worship, scattering flowers and burning incense.”
"May I attain such a physical body as this," [he thinks] as he practices generosity,
maintains the precepts, and performs various meritorious deeds for the sake of attaining the subtle and wonderful body of a Tathāgata. Thus it is, Mañjuśrī!
"The Tathāgata’s supernatural power appears in the world to bring great benefit to all sentient beings; like a shadow or a reflection, it manifests according to what sentient beings perceive.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The Tathāgata is eternally abiding, Neither born nor extinguished, Neither mind nor form."
Neither existent nor non-existent;
like the reflection of a palace seen upon a lapis lazuli floor, this reflection is not existent, yet it is likewise not non-existent.
When the minds of sentient beings are pure, they see the body of the Tathāgata; that it is neither existent nor non-existent is likewise so. “Mañjuśrī!
Just as when the sun first rises it first illuminates the high mountains, then reaches the middle mountains, and finally shines upon the lower lands;
so too is the Tathāgata: devoid of mind, intellect, and consciousness; signless and free from signs; having severed all signs;
neither clinging to that nor clinging to this; not dwelling on this shore, not dwelling on the other shore, and not dwelling in the middle stream.
It is inconceivable, beyond the reach of thought; neither high nor low; without bondage and without liberation;
neither possessing wisdom nor lacking wisdom; neither affliction nor non-affliction;
neither real nor unreal; neither knowledge nor non-knowledge; inconceivable yet not inconceivable.
Neither practicing nor not practicing, neither mindfulness nor non-mindfulness,
neither mind nor non-mind, neither intellect nor non-intellect, neither name nor non-name, neither form nor formlessness;
without grasping and without non-grasping, neither speaking nor not speaking, neither expressible nor inexpressible, neither visible nor...
It is invisible; it is neither a guide nor not a guide, neither one who has attained the fruit nor one who has not attained the fruit.

Thus it is, Mañjuśrī! The radiant light of the Tathāgata’s sun of wisdom shines upon the triple world: first it illuminates the bodhisattvas, as if shining upon a high mountain; next it illuminates those who delight in the paths of pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas; and finally it illuminates those who delight in roots of goodness, even down to sentient beings fixed in error, in order to increase their wholesome dharmas and to give rise to causes and conditions for the future.
“Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata is equal, without superior, middle, or inferior, and always practices the mind of equanimity. Mañjuśrī!”
The Tathāgata does not entertain such thoughts as:
"To these sentient beings I shall preach the superior Dharma; to those sentient beings I shall preach the non-superior Dharma. Nor does he think:
"This sentient being has a great intention; this sentient being has a middling intention; this sentient being has a small intention;
this one delights in wholesome dharmas; this one delights in unwholesome dharmas;
this person is fixed in the right determination; this person is fixed in the wrong determination."
The light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom does not engage in such discrimination, for he has already severed all conceptualizations of discrimination.
Because sentient beings possess various roots of goodness, the wisdom of the Tathāgata appears in various ways accordingly.

“Mañjuśrī! It is like a maṇi jewel in the great ocean called ‘Fulfilling the Wishes of All Sentient Beings,’ which is placed atop a banner and provides whatever sentient beings require; yet that maṇi jewel has no mind, thought, or consciousness.”
The Tathāgata is likewise without mind, thought, or consciousness;
he is immeasurable, unattainable, ungraspable, and inexpressible. He has eliminated all afflictions and ignorance;
he is neither real nor unreal, neither permanent nor impermanent, neither luminous nor non-luminous, and neither worldly nor...

It is not of the world; it is without applied thought and sustained reflection; it is neither arising nor ceasing; it is inconceivable; it is without mind and without substance; it is unmoving and non-active; it is immeasurable and boundless;
it is ineffable and beyond speech; it is without joy and without lack of joy; it is numberless and transcends all numbering; it is without going and without coming; it has no place of abiding.
It cuts off all realms of existence; it is invisible and ungraspable; it is free from conceptual construction; it is neither empty nor non-empty;
it is neither a combination nor a non-combination; it is inconceivable and unknowable;
it is neither defiled nor pure; it is neither name nor form; it is neither karma nor its fruit; it is neither past nor future.
It does not come from the present; it is non-existent, soundless, signless, and free from all signs.
It is neither internal, nor external, nor in between. Thus it is, Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgata dwells in purity upon the banner of great compassion; according to the inclinations of sentient beings, he manifests various bodies and teaches various dharmas. “Mañjuśrī!
Just as an echo arises from sound, being neither internal nor external, nor in between, neither arising nor ceasing, neither interrupted nor permanent—Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is likewise:
neither internal nor external, nor in between; neither arising nor ceasing, nameless and signless, yet manifesting in various ways according to the needs of sentient beings.
“Mañjuśrī! Just as all grasses and trees grow depending upon the earth, and that earth is impartial and free from all discrimination;

so too do the roots of goodness of all sentient beings grow depending upon the Tathāgata. Whether they belong to the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Bodhisattva vehicle—even the roots of goodness of all non-Buddhists, such as the naked Nirgranthas—likewise grow depending upon the Tathāgata.”
The Tathāgata’s equanimity and lack of discrimination are likewise thus.

"Mañjuśrī! Just as space is equal and without inferior, middling, or superior, so too is the Tathāgata’s equanimity; it is only sentient beings who perceive themselves as having inferior, middling, or superior [capacities]."
Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata does not form such thoughts as:

"This being has an inferior intention, so I shall manifest an inferior body; for this being with a middling intention, I shall manifest a middling-superior body; to this being with an inferior intention, I shall teach the Hīnayāna; to this being with a middling intention, I shall teach the Pratyekabuddha and Śrāvaka vehicles; and to this being with a superior intention, I shall teach the Mahāyāna."
"Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata does not have such a thought as:
'This sentient being delights in giving; I shall speak of giving; and likewise for morality, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom.'"
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is equal, being free from mind, intellect, and consciousness, and thus devoid of discrimination. “Mañjuśrī!

All dharmas are entirely equal; because they are equal, they have no abiding; because they have no abiding, they have no movement; because they have no movement, they have no dependence; because they have no dependence, they have no location; because they have no location, they do not arise; because they do not arise, they do not cease.

If one can see in this way, the mind is not inverted; because it is not inverted, it is as it truly is; because it is as it truly is, there is no activity; because there is no activity, there is no coming; because there is no coming, there is no going; because there is no going, it is suchness (*tathatā*); because it is suchness, it accords with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); because it accords with the nature of phenomena, it is immovable. If one accords with the nature of phenomena and is immovable, then one attains the nature of phenomena; if one attains the nature of phenomena, then there is no longing.
Why is this? Because they have already attained the Way.
If one attains the Way, one does not abide in any phenomena (*dharmas*); because one does not abide in any phenomena, there is neither arising nor ceasing, neither name nor mark.
“Mañjuśrī! If sentient beings are attached to all phenomena, they give rise to afflictions; because they give rise to afflictions, they do not attain bodhi.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is bodhi attained? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Without root and without location, this is how the Tathāgata attains bodhi.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What constitutes a root?"
"What is its basis? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"The view of a self-identity is the root; unreal reflection is the basis."
Mañjuśrī! The wisdom of the Tathāgata is equal to bodhi and equal to all dharmas; therefore, being without root and without location, this is the attainment of bodhi.
Mañjuśrī! Awakening is quiescent. In what way is it quiescent?
There is inner tranquility and outer tranquility.

Why is this? The eye is empty; it is neither self nor belonging to a self. The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty; they are neither self nor belonging to a self. Because one knows the eye is empty, one does not engage with forms; this is called tranquility.
In this way, one knows that the ear is empty and does not engage with sounds; this is called tranquility.
It is the same for knowing that the nose, and so forth, up to the mind, are empty. Mañjuśrī!
“Bodhi is neither moving nor proceeding;
that which does not move does not grasp at any phenomena, and that which does not proceed does not abandon any phenomena. Mañjuśrī!...”

The Tathāgata is immovable; thus he is as it truly is. To be as it truly is means not seeing this shore and not seeing the other shore. Because he does not see "this" or "that," he sees all dharmas. Because he sees all dharmas, he is called the Tathāgata.
“Mañjuśrī! Awakening (bodhi) is without marks and without conditions.
In what way is it without marks?
What is meant by "without object"?
Not apprehending eye-consciousness is signlessness; not seeing forms is being without object.
Not apprehending ear-consciousness is signlessness; not hearing sounds is being without object.
This applies even to the mind and mental phenomena (*dharmas*). "Mañjuśrī!
Awakening (*bodhi*) does not belong to the three periods of time—past, future, or present; it is the equal severance of the流转 (*saṃsāra*, cyclic flow) of these three times."
Mañjuśrī! How does one sever the flow of saṃsāra?

By not giving rise to future consciousness from the past mind, by not engaging the present mentation, and by being unmoving and non-abiding, not conceptualizing, not perceiving, and not discriminating.
Mañjuśrī! Bodhi is formless and unconditioned.
In what way is it formless?
Is it because it cannot be cognized by the six consciousnesses?
How is it unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
Because it is without arising, abiding, and ceasing; this is called severing the flow of the three periods of time.
“Mañjuśrī! Bodhi is an indestructible phrase. Why is it indestructible?
What is the phrase?
That which is signless is indestructible; suchness is the phrase.
That which has no abiding place is indestructible; the dharma-realm is the phrase.
Immovability is indestructible; emptiness is its phrase.
Non-attainment is indestructible; signlessness is its phrase.
Non-perception is indestructible; non-action is its phrase.
Non-expectation is non-disruption; the absence of intrinsic nature is the phrase.
That sentient beings lack intrinsic nature is non-disruption; space is the phrase.
Unattainability is non-disruption; non-arising is the phrase.
Non-extinction is indestructible; it is the phrase of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Non-practice is indestructible; it is the phrase of awakening (*bodhi*).
Quiescence is indestructible; it is the phrase of nirvāṇa.
That which does not arise again is indestructible; non-arising is the phrase. “Mañjuśrī!
Bodhi cannot be awakened to by means of the body, nor can it be awakened to by means of the mind.”
Why is this? Because the body is insentient, like grass and wood; and the mind is deceptive, being unreal. Mañjuśrī!
If one claims that bodhi is that which is realized by body and mind, this relies on conventional designations and is not the ultimate meaning. Why?
Because bodhi is neither body nor mind, and is neither empty nor substantial.
Mañjuśrī! Awakening cannot be expressed in words. Why is this?
Just as space has no location, being neither born nor extinguished and devoid of names; so too, Mañjuśrī,
the reality of all phenomena is ineffable.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are not real, are beyond verbal expression, and are neither born nor extinguished. "Mañjuśrī!..."
Bodhi is that which cannot be grasped and has no location.
Why is it ungraspable and without location?
Eye-consciousness cannot be grasped, and the non-apprehension of form constitutes its lack of location.
Auditory consciousness cannot be grasped; because sound is not apprehended, it has no locus.
This is likewise for the nose up to the mind and its objects.
As for bodhi, it cannot be awakened to; because the eye does not grasp, form is not apprehended, and because form is not apprehended, consciousness has no place of abiding.
Because the ear does not grasp, it does not apprehend sound; because it does not apprehend sound, consciousness has no place of abiding.
This applies likewise up to the mind and mental phenomena. "Mañjuśrī!..."
Bodhi is explained as emptiness, because all dharmas are empty; this emptiness is what the Tathāgata knows, and this emptiness is what the Tathāgata has awakened to.
Mañjuśrī! It is not from emptiness that emptiness exists; this is what has been awakened to by the Tathāgata. Why is this?
Because it is signless. "Furthermore, Mañjuśrī,
the wisdom that is the cause of bodhi is also emptiness."
Why is this? Because it is signless (*animitta*). Mañjuśrī!

Emptiness and bodhi are both utterly non-existent; they are neither dual nor plural, nameless and signless, transcending mind, intellect, and consciousness; they are neither born nor extinguished, without activity and without location, and are neither sound nor speech.
Mañjuśrī! It is spoken of merely by way of names; in reality, it cannot be spoken of. "Mañjuśrī! [he said].

The Tathāgata fully knows that all dharmas, from the very beginning, are neither born nor arisen, neither exhausted nor extinguished; they are without name or mark, and are beyond mind, thought, and consciousness. Because he knows them thus, he is liberated thus: he is neither bound nor liberated.
“Mañjuśrī! Bodhi is equal to space. Space is neither unequal nor not unequal.”
Enlightenment is neither equal nor unequal.
Such is the characteristic of phenomena as realized by the Tathāgata, Mañjuśrī!
"Just as the atom of an anu is neither equal nor unequal, so too are all dharmas; one who possesses true wisdom knows them in this way. Mañjuśrī!"
How does true wisdom know all phenomena such that those not yet arisen arise, and having arisen, they immediately perish?
Because all those phenomena are without arising and are not grasped.

“Mañjuśrī! Bodhi is the reality-limit (bhūta-koṭi). That which is the reality-limit does not depart from the reality-limit in accordance with the characteristics of bodhi; form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not depart from the reality-limit.

Just as the characteristic of bodhi does not depart from the reality-limit, so too the earth element does not depart from the reality-limit, and the water, fire, and wind elements do not depart from the reality-limit.”

Just as the characteristics of awakening—the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element—are not separate from suchness, so too, up to the mind element, the phenomena element, and the mind-consciousness element, they are not separate from suchness; this is called the phrase of suchness.
“Mañjuśrī! Awakening is entering into non-practice through practice. Mañjuśrī!”
What is practice? What is non-practice?
Practice consists in taking all wholesome dharmas as objects; non-practice consists in not obtaining any wholesome dharmas.
The practitioner’s mind does not abide; for one who is no longer a practitioner, there is liberation through signlessness.
The practitioner can be measured, but the one who is no longer a practitioner cannot be measured.
Why cannot they be measured?
Because it is unrecognizable.
Mañjuśrī, awakening (bodhi) is without outflows and without grasping; "without outflows" means that the four currents have been extinguished.

What are the four? They are the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance. To be unattached to these four floods is called the extinction of the four floods.
One who is without grasping extinguishes the four kinds of grasping.
What are the four graspings?
Grasping at sense-pleasures, grasping at views, grasping at precepts and observances, and grasping at the doctrine of self; these are called the four graspings.
"All these appropriations are darkened by ignorance and deceived by craving, because they arise through mutual succession.

Mañjuśrī! By means of the knowledge of reality as it is, one cuts off the root of the appropriation of self-theory; because the root of appropriation is cut off, the body attains purity, and that which is pure in body is without arising or ceasing."

Mañjuśrī! That which is without arising or ceasing does not give rise to mind, thought, or consciousness; it does not engage in conceptualization or discrimination. If there were discrimination, it would constitute ignorance.

If this ignorance does not arise, then there are no twelve links of dependent origination; the absence of the twelve links of dependent origination is non-arising; non-arising is the Path; the Path is the definitive meaning; the definitive meaning is the ultimate truth; the ultimate truth is the meaning of non-self; the meaning of non-self is the meaning of the ineffable; the meaning of the ineffable is the meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination; the meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination is the meaning of the Dharma; and the meaning of the Dharma is the meaning of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, I say that if one sees the twelve links of dependent origination, this is seeing the Dharma; seeing the Dharma is seeing the Buddha; such seeing is non-seeing.
“Mañjuśrī! Awakening is pure, stainless, and free from afflictions. Mañjuśrī!”
Emptiness is purity; signlessness is stainlessness; wishlessness is the absence of affliction.
Furthermore, non-arising is purity; the unconditioned is stainlessness; non-ceasing is the absence of affliction.
Furthermore, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is purity; purity is stainlessness (*vimala*); and stainlessness is the absence of afflictions (*anāsrava*).
Furthermore, non-discrimination is purity; the absence of discrimination is stainlessness; and the cessation of discrimination is the absence of afflictions.
Suchness is purity; the dharma-realm is stainless; true contemplation is free from affliction.
Space is purity; space is stainless; space is free from affliction.
Knowledge of the internal body is purity; internal conduct is stainlessness; not apprehending either internal or external is the absence of affliction.
Knowing the aggregates (*skandha*) is purity; the intrinsic nature of the elements (*dhātu*) is stainlessness; not abandoning the sense bases (*āyatana*) is the absence of affliction.

The knowledge of exhaustion regarding the past is purity; the knowledge of non-arising regarding the future is stainlessness; the knowledge of the dharma-realm regarding the present is the absence of affliction. Mañjuśrī!
This is called pure, stainless, and free from affliction; this is itself tranquility.
Tranquility means inner and outer tranquility; that which is both inner and outer tranquil is great tranquility, and because of this great tranquility, one is called a Muni.
Mañjuśrī! As space is bodhi, so is bodhi all dharmas; as all dharmas are all sentient beings, so are all sentient beings the objective realm; and as the objective realm is nirvāṇa.

“Mañjuśrī! All dharmas are equal to nirvāṇa; because they are supreme and boundless, they have no antidote. Because they have no antidote, they are primordially pure, primordially stainless, and primordially free from afflictions.”

Mañjuśrī! Thus, having awakened to all dharmas, the Tathāgata contemplates all sentient beings and gives rise to great compassion, causing them to sport in the realm that is pure, stainless, and free from affliction.
“Mañjuśrī! How do the bodhisattvas practice the bodhisattva path? Mañjuśrī!”
The Bodhisattva does not engage in discursive thought; he does not act for the sake of cessation, nor for the sake of arising. This is what it means to practice the conduct of a Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, the past mind of a Bodhisattva has already ceased and thus does not function; the future mind has not yet arrived and thus does not function; and although the present mind exists, it likewise does not function.
Why is this? Because they do not cling to the past, the future, or the present. Mañjuśrī!
This is called a bodhisattva practicing the bodhisattva path. "Mañjuśrī!
Generosity and the Tathāgata are without two distinct characteristics; this is what the bodhisattva practices."
In this way, morality, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom, as well as the non-duality of the Tathāgata, constitute the practice of a bodhisattva. “Mañjuśrī!
If a bodhisattva does not practice that form is empty, nor does he practice that form is not empty, this is the bodhisattva’s practice.”
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of form is empty.
In this way, the bodhisattva does not engage with the emptiness or non-emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva. Why?
Because mind, thought, and consciousness cannot be apprehended.
Mañjuśrī! All dharmas are non-existent; they should be cultivated and realized. If one realizes them, then neither afflictions arise nor do afflictions cease.
Mañjuśrī! Arising and ceasing are spoken of as provisional names; within the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), there is neither arising nor ceasing. Mañjuśrī!

Suppose all sentient beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth—whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception, two-legged, four-legged, many-legged, or legless—were all to attain a human body. Having attained a human body, they would each give rise to the bodhicitta. Once they had given rise to the bodhicitta, each and every bodhisattva would, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as to bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas, providing them with food, drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, and all manner of articles of comfort. This would continue until after their entry into parinirvāṇa, at which time stupas made of the seven precious gems, one hundred yojanas in height, would be erected; these would be covered by jeweled canopies and adorned with suspended maṇi jewels, and draped with various banners and canopies, with *vaijayanta* maṇi jewels forming a lattice-work around them.

If there is a bodhisattva who, with a pure mind, hears this *Sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālaṃkārasūtra*, and having heard it, joyfully receives, maintains, believes, and understands it, even going so far as to explain a single verse or a single phrase to others, their merit shall surpass the former merit by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a ten-thousandfold, a hundred-millionfold, and even beyond what can be reached by calculation or analogy.
Why is this? Because this sutra extensively expounds the inconceivable, pure, signless, and subtle Dharma-body. Mañjuśrī!

If there were as many bodhisattvas as the sands of the Ganges, and as many Buddha-worlds as the sands of the Ganges, all fashioned from Jambūnada gold—even the trees, flowers, and fruits being made of Jambūnada gold—and adorned with celestial garments upon those trees, covered above by nets of all-luminous maṇi jewels, with Vaijayanta maṇi jewels forming the palaces and vidyutprabha maṇi jewels forming the steps and thresholds, and with various precious banners suspended; if one were to daily offer such things to as many Buddhas as the sands of the Ganges for countless kalpas.

If there is a bodhisattva who maintains right mindfulness of this sutra, or even proclaims a single verse from it, the merit of the former bodhisattvas’ practice of giving does not equal one hundredth part of this merit; it does not equal one part in a hundred thousand million billion, nor can it be reached by any calculation or analogy. Thus, all other merits whatsoever cannot compare with the merit of this sutra.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this geya:
"If there are those who receive and uphold this subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Dharma-body,
the merit and benefits they obtain shall be beyond measure."
Suppose all sentient beings were to be born in the human realm,
and together they were to resolve upon the mind of enlightenment in pursuit of all-knowledge;
such bodhisattvas would all become great donors.
With various kinds of offerings, they made worship to countless Buddhas,
as well as to the Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas,
until their entry into parinirvāṇa; for each, they erected stupas made of the seven precious substances.
Reaching a height of a hundred yojanas, adorned with various kinds of jewels;
yet if a person upholds this sutra, or even recites a single verse from it,
the merit they produce will surpass this, being immeasurable and boundless.
Because this sutra explains the form-body of signlessness,
those who possess wisdom should therefore mindfully receive and uphold it,
read and recite it, copy it, and offer flowers and incense as worship.
The fruit of the merit thus obtained is inconceivable;
before long, one shall proceed to the site of enlightenment, subdue Māra, and realize perfect awakening.
Such sūtras as these are praised by all Buddhas.
"This is the wondrous Dharma-body, signless and beyond words;
therefore, for those who uphold it, the merit is immeasurable.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Mañjuśrī and all the other bodhisattvas, the immeasurable pratyekabuddhas and the assembly of śrāvakas, as well as the entire multitude of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
